title: Celsus’s two choices
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις φησὶν ὁ Κέλσος· δυοῖν θάτερον αἱρεῖ λόγος. εἰ μὲν ἀπαξιοῦσι θεραπεύειν τὰ εἰκότα τούτων δὲ ἐπιστάτας, μήτ᾿ εἰς ἀνδρὸς ἰέναι μήτ᾿ ἄγεσθαι γυναῖκα μήτ᾿ ἀναιρεῖσθαι τέκνα μήτ᾿ ἄλλο πράττειν μηδὲν ἐν τῷ βίῳ. χωρεῖν δ᾿ ἔνθεν πασσυδὶ μηδὲν σπέρμα ἐλλειπομένους. ὡς αν ἐρημωθείη πάμπαν ἐπὶ γῆς τὸ τοιοῦτον γένος· εἰ δὲ καὶ γυναῖκας ἄξονται καὶ παῖδας ποιήσονται καὶ καρπῶν γεύσονται καὶ τῶν ἐν τῷ βίῳ μεθέξουσι καὶ κακῶν τῶν ἐπιτεταγμένων ἀνέξονται (φύσις μὲν γὰρ αὕτη πάντας ἀνθρώπους πειρᾶσθαι κακῶν· εἶναι μὲν γὰρ ἀνάγκη κακὰ, χώραν δ᾿ ἄλλην οὐκ ἔχει), ἀποδοτέον δὴ τὰς προσηκούσας τοῖς ταῦτ᾿ ἐπιτετραμμένοις τιμὰς καὶ τῷ βίῳ λειτουργητέον τὰ πρέποντα. μέχρι ἂν τῶν δεσμῶν ἀπολυθῶσι, μὴ καὶ ἀχάριστοι πρὸς τούσδε εἶναι δοκῶσι. καὶ γὰρ ἄδικον μετέχοντας ὧν οἵδε ἔχουσι μηδὲν αὐτοῖς συντελεῖν. φαμὲν δὲ καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα ὅτι εὔλογος ἐξαγωγὴ οὐδεμία ἡμῖν εἶναι δοκεῖ εἰ μὴ ἡ δι᾿ εὐσέβειαν καὶ ἀρετὴν μόνη. ἐπὰν ὑπὸ τῶν δικάζειν νομιζομένων ἢ ἐξουσίαν τοῦ ζῆν ἡμῶν ἔχειν δοκούντων τὸ ἕτερον προτείνηται, ἢ τὸ ζῆν μετὰ τοῦ παρὰ τὰ διατεταγμένα ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πράττειν ἢ τὸ ἀποθνῄσκειν μετὰ τοῦ πείθεσθαι τοῖς λόγοις αὐτοῦ. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄγεσθαι γυναῖκα ἐπέτρεψεν ἡμῖν ὁ θεὸς, ὡς οὐ πάντων χωρούντων τὸ διαφέρον τουτέστι τὸ πάντῃ καθαρὸν, καὶ ἀγομένοις γυναῖκας τὰ γεννώμενα πάντως τρέφειν καὶ μὴ ἀναιρεῖν τὰ ὑπὸ τῆς προνοίας διδόμενα τέκνα. καὶ οὐ μάχεται ταῦτα τῷ μὴ πείθεσθαι ἡμᾶς τοῖς νεμομένοις τὴν γῆν δαιμονίοις· ὁπλισάμενοι γὰρ τῇ πανοπλίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ ἱστάμεθα ὡς ἀθληταὶ εὐσεβείας πρὸς τὸ τῶν ἐπιβουλευόντων ἡμῖν δαιμόνων γένος.
pass_a_gloss: Next to these Celsus says: reason (λόγος) chooses (αἱρέω) one of two. If they disdain (ἀπαξιόω) to serve (θεραπεύω) the fitting things the overseers (ἐπιστάτης) of these, neither to go to a man's [house] nor to take (ἄγομαι) a wife nor to take up children nor to do anything else in life (βίος); but to depart (χωρέω) hence all together (πασσυδί) leaving behind (ἐλλείπω) no seed (σπέρμα), so that such a race (γένος) might be made desolate (ἐρημόω) altogether (πάμπαν) upon earth. But if they will take wives and make children and taste (γεύομαι) fruits (καρπός) and partake (μετέχω) of the things in life and endure (ἀνέχομαι) the evils (κακά) enjoined/appointed (ἐπιτάσσω) (for this is nature (φύσις): all men experience (πειράομαι) evils; for evils must (ἀνάγκη) exist, and have no other place (χώρα)), one must render (ἀποδίδωμι) the fitting (προσήκω) honours (τιμή) to those entrusted (ἐπιτρέπω) with these, and minister (λειτουργέω) to life the things befitting (πρέπω), until they are released (ἀπολύω) from the bonds (δεσμός), lest they seem ungrateful (ἀχάριστος) toward them. For it is unjust (ἄδικος) partaking of what they have to contribute (συντελέω) nothing to them. We say to this that no reasonable exit seems to us to be except only that for piety (εὐσέβεια) and virtue (ἀρετή), when by those thought (νομίζω) to judge (δικάζω) or seeming to have authority (ἐξουσία) over our living, one of the two is put forward (προτείνω): either to live with doing contrary to things ordained (διατάσσω) by Jesus, or to die with obeying (πείθομαι) his words. But God also permitted (ἐπιτρέπω) us to take a wife, as not all making room for/receiving (χωρέω) the excellent, that is, the wholly pure, and for those taking wives by all means (πάντως) to rear (τρέφω) the things begotten (γεννάω) and not to destroy (ἀναιρέω) the children given (δίδωμι) by providence (πρόνοια). And these do not fight against (μάχομαι) our not obeying the demons (δαιμόνιον) who hold/graze (νέμομαι) the earth; for armed (ὁπλίζω) with the full armour (πανοπλία) of God we stand (ἵσταμαι) as athletes (ἀθλητής) of piety against the race of demons plotting against (ἐπιβουλεύω) us.
pass_b_english: Next Celsus says: “Reason makes us choose one of two courses. If they refuse to give the overseers of these things the service that befits them, then they should neither take a husband nor take a wife nor raise children nor do anything else in life, but depart from here one and all, leaving no seed behind, so that such a race might be wholly wiped out from the earth. But if they are going to take wives and have children and taste the fruits and share in the things of life and bear the evils appointed for them — for this is the way of nature, that all men experience evils; for evils must exist, and they have no other place (see Plato, Theaetetus 176a) — then they must render the fitting honours to those who have been entrusted with these things, and perform the duties that befit life until they are released from their bonds, so that they may not also seem ungrateful toward these beings. For it is unjust to share in what they possess and contribute nothing to them.”

To this too we say that no departure from life seems reasonable to us except that alone which is for the sake of piety and virtue: when those who are thought to sit as judges, or who seem to have power over our life, set before us one of two things, either to live while doing what is contrary to the commands of Jesus, or to die while obeying his words.

But God has also allowed us to marry, since not all can receive what is better, that is, complete purity (Matthew 19:11); and he has charged those who marry to rear without fail what is born to them, and not to destroy the children given by providence. And this does not conflict with our refusal to obey the demons who have the earth as their domain; for, armed with the whole armour of God (Ephesians 6:11), we stand as athletes of piety against the race of demons that plot against us.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words run from ‘Reason makes us choose’ to ‘contribute nothing to them’. The phrase θεραπεύειν τὰ εἰκότα τούτων δὲ ἐπιστάτας is grammatically awkward in the staged text (likely corrupt); rendered by the evident sense, ‘give the overseers of these things the service that befits them’. εἰς ἀνδρὸς ἰέναι is the idiom for a woman going to a husband’s house, paired with ἄγεσθαι γυναῖκα for a man; rendered ‘take a husband nor take a wife’ to keep the pairing without the calque ‘go to a husband’. ἀναιρεῖσθαι τέκνα (middle) means to take up, that is, acknowledge and raise, newborns; Origen answers with the active ἀναιρεῖν, ‘destroy’, of exposure or infanticide, a play the English shows by ‘raise’ versus ‘destroy’. ‘Evils must exist, and they have no other place’ echoes Plato, Theaetetus 176a (evils can neither perish nor dwell among the gods, but haunt mortal nature and this region); cited with ‘see’ because Celsus paraphrases. εὔλογος ἐξαγωγή (‘reasonable departure from life’) is the Stoic term for justified suicide; Origen grants it only for martyrdom. ἐπέτρεψεν governs both clauses: ‘allowed’ for marriage and ‘charged’ for rearing children, since ἐπιτρέπω covers permit and enjoin. ‘Not all can receive’ (οὐ πάντων χωρούντων) echoes Matthew 19:11; 1 Corinthians 7 stands behind the permission to marry but is not quoted, so it is not cited. Ephesians 6:11 (also 6:13) for the full armour of God.
εἰς ἀνδρὸς ἰέναι: calque 'go to a husband' -> 'take a husband'

Celsus's parenthesis: 'this is nature, that all men should have experience of evils' -> 'this is the way of nature, that all men experience evils'; second γάρ restored ('for evils must exist'); 'there is no other place for them' -> 'they have no other place' (subject κακά)
καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα: 'To this' -> 'To this too'
Celsus/Origen boundary, Plato Theaetetus 176a echo, Matthew 19:11 and Ephesians 6:11 checked
